newsitem.title: UK: Czech coffee use to level out after rise - Douwe.
newsitem.headline: Czech coffee use to level out after rise - Douwe.

text.p: After a strong rise in 1996, coffee consumption in the Czech Republic could stay flat in 1997 following this year's steep rally in bean prices, said an official at Czech coffee firm Balirny Douwe Egberts a.s.
After stagnating at around 23,000 tonnes in 1995, consumption expanded by seven percent to 24,700 last year. It rose further in early 1997 but a fall could be expected in the second half of the year.
"On balance, it will be a flat growth this year after the big increases in raw material prices," Peter Sorenson, marketing director of the Prague-based firm, told Reuters by telephone.
Balirny Douwe Egberts is part of the Dutch Sara Lee/DE group, which in turned is owned by the giant Sara Lee Corp of the United States.
Sara Lee/DE acquired Czech firm Prazirny a Balirny Praha in March 1992.
Sorenson said there had been a 10 percent rise in retail coffee prices in the Central European state so far this year following the rising cost of beans from Central and Latin America.
Strikes by Colombian truck drivers and dock workers had affected supply. There have also been forecasts of a much lower crop from Brazil this coming season.
Since early January, arabica coffee futures on the New York exchange have doubled to $2.30 a lb, basis the second-month contract.
Other major roasters from the United States and Western Europe have also put up prices on the supermarket shelves at least twice this year.
Sorenson said Balirny's sales volume had risen to around 1.0 billion crowns from 880 million in 1993, its first full financial year.
But its market share had been fluctuating due to keen competition from two other Western firms -- German roaster Tchibo, and Jacobs, a division of the U.S.-based Philip Morris Co Inc.
Sorenson said the latest data from the Nielsen market research firm put Balirny's market share of local coffee and tea sales at 28 percent.
The bulk of Czech imports are arabica coffee, the higher premium coffee.

According to opinion polls, roasted coffee is still the preferred hot beverage in the Czech Republic, accounting for 86 percent of the market. This is followed by tea at 10 percent and instant coffee at four percent.
The latter is the fastest-growing sector, expanding by 10 to 15 percent a year.
Statistics show that 94 percent of the country's households buy coffee at least once a year and 60 percent of the consumers find big differences between coffee brands, he said.
Most Czechs still prefer to drink a local version of Turkish coffee, known as "turek" -- boiling water poured on to finely-ground roasted coffee, stirred and then left to settle.
This is the lowest-quality method of making coffee as the more expensive coffee machines are still beyond the means of average consumers.
